newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-SHOWCASE-GULLIT RELAXES INTO FIRST YEAR IN MANAGEMENT.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-SHOWCASE-GULLIT RELAXES INTO FIRST YEAR IN MANAGEMENT.

text.p: Enviably relaxed both on and off the field, Chelsea player-manager Ruud Gullit has brought a new approach to the neurotic world of British soccer management.
"His style of management is certainly different," said Steve Clarke, Chelsea's longest-serving first team player who has seen half a dozen bosses in his time at the club.
"He's a lot more laid back than most. He doesn't try to ram things down your throat. He treats players like adults."
Gullit says he has never been inclined to leap about or yell no matter how nerve racking the match is or how badly his players are performing.

"Every game I am tense. I just express myself in different way," he said. "Then in the dressing room if you want to make a point you make it clearly without fuss. Anyway it looks silly if a foreigner tries to shout in English."
Gullit is the first foreign manager to take a team to the F.A.Cup final, a fact which leaves him profoundly unimpressed.
While his domestic players are beside themselves with excitement at the chance of lifting the Cup for the first time since 1970,, Gullit remains cool.
"For me I was taught in Italy that the champions' league was the ultimate goal...then you have the chance to be the best team in Europe," the Dutchman said.

As a player Gullit, 34, has won practically every honour going, from the European championship as captain of the Netherlands to the European Cup with AC Milan, picking up European Footballer of the Year on the way.
He started in 1978 with Harlem and made his international debut on his 19th birthday. In 1982 he moved to Feyenoord and was transferred to PSV Einhoven three years later.

In 1987 he signed for AC Milan for a world record $8.4 million and won three league titles with them before joining Sampdoria in 1993. In 1994 he moved back to Milan before rejoining Samdoria until his transfer to Glenn Hoddle's Chelsea two years ago. He scored 16 goals for the Netherlands in 66 appearanced.
Though he finds playing and managing a difficult juggling act and has appeared in few games this season, his influence with the players derives in part from the respect they have for his ability.
Though past his peak and plagued by injury he still possesses sublime skills, can pass perfectly and terrorise any midfield.
His powerful attacking runs, dreadlocks flying, has brought him adulation in the Netherlands in Italy and now in south west London.

As a world class mixed race player -- his mother is Dutch and father from Surinam -- he has also been a role model for young black players round the globe. Former Ireland manager Jackie Charlton dubbed him "The compelete modern footballer."

Such a pedigree ensured that when he took over from Hoddle, who took over the England job last year, Gullit could entice top European players such as Italians Gianfranco Zola, Roberto Di Matteo and Gianluca Vialli and French sweeper Frank Leboeuf to Stamford Bridge.

Though still a fledgling manager Gullit has managed to get the best from his players. The magical Zola has been voted the English league's player of the year and the Italians have transmitted their passing skills to the domestic players, who are thriving on fast-moving, entertaining -- if sometimes a little erratic -- continental football.
"You have to stimulate players and give them some freedom. The talent comes out then," Gullit said as he prepared his team for the Cup final.

Gullit's aim now is for more consistency from the squad. "If you look at the points we dropped early in the season, you can see we could have finished in the top three," he said. Chelsea ended sixth, just outside the UEFA Cup places.
"But the last couple of games we did not give stupid goals away so things are changing already," he added.
Gullit fell into management, prematurely and almost by chance, an apparently inspired though at the time not entirely confident choice by Chelsea's directors.
"I never thought of being a manager. I'd thought about perhaps training youngsters but then they gave me the job and I've had to learn quickly -- and I'm still learning," he said.
"My first year I've enjoyed very much. If I continue enjoying it as much then I will carry on."
